summary: Discusses design considerations for making Internet protocols extensible, aimed at people designing base protocols and their extensions. It uses case studies to show what works and what causes trouble. A companion document, RFC 4775, covers the procedures for extending protocols. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Protocol extensions can add needed features, but poorly designed ones can make systems incompatible or less secure. This RFC gives designers principles for allowing protocols to evolve safely.

questions: how do protocol extensions cause interoperability failures
what is the difference between routine and major extensions
subtitle: Design principles for extending Internet protocols without breaking interoperability

tldr.problem: Extensions let protocols evolve, but can create incompatible variants, security gaps and operational problems when they conflict with the base protocol or existing implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC distinguishes routine from major extensions and gives architectural principles and base-protocol design guidance for interoperability, testing, parameter registration and security.
tldr.outcome: This Informational IAB document is a design guide. Its companion RFC 4775 describes procedures for protocol extensions and variations.

today: RFC 6709 is an Informational document from the Internet Architecture Board, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion, RFC 4775, covers protocol-extension procedures.

sections.title: Why Protocols Need Careful Extensions
sections.content:
Protocols often include ways to add features later. Well-designed extensions can support incremental changes while allowing systems with different capabilities to interoperate. But each extension adds implementation, deployment and compatibility costs, and may introduce security or operational risks.

This RFC discusses design considerations for base protocols and their extensions. Formal procedures for extending IETF protocols are covered separately by RFC 4775. The document recommends reading the full discussion because its design considerations are connected.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols need ways to change as new needs arise. Designers must make sure an added feature does not break systems that do not use it.

sections.title: Routine and Major Extensions
sections.content:
A major extension may require changes to the base protocol or deployed implementations, change architectural assumptions or syntax, introduce new usage patterns, affect multiple protocols, alter security or affect performance. Such changes need careful review of backward compatibility and operational effects.

A routine extension does not require changes to the base protocol or existing implementations, and those implementations can safely ignore it. DHCP vendor-specific options and RADIUS vendor-specific attributes are examples. Even routine extensions can benefit from expert review, especially if their data format is difficult to process.
sections.plainLanguage: A routine extension can be ignored safely by systems that do not use it. A major extension may require changes or affect how the protocol works, so it needs closer review.

sections.title: Principles for Extensible Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC gives seven principles: limit extensibility to what is reasonably anticipated; design for global interoperability; fit extensions to the base protocol's architecture; avoid incompatible variations; make extension behavior testable; coordinate parameter assignments; and take special care when extending critical protocols.

Private or experimental values are not suitable for Internet-wide use because different sites may assign them incompatible meanings. They should remain within the domain where their meaning is controlled. The RFC also warns that extensions should not create incompatible protocol forks or silently depend on mechanisms that the base protocol does not define.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep extension mechanisms focused, documented and testable. Coordinate new values so that two developers do not assign different meanings to the same value.

sections.title: Prepare the Base Protocol for Change
sections.content:
A base protocol should say how peers negotiate extensions, how unknown extensions are handled and whether an extended implementation can find a useful common feature set with an unextended peer. Version-number schemes need explicit behavior for versions a receiver does not recognize.

Reserved fields should specify what senders transmit and what receivers do with other values; a field marked “must be zero” should normally be ignored on receipt so a future use does not break older implementations. Designers should also provide enough parameter space, clear encoding rules and cryptographic agility where needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The base specification should explain how peers agree on features and what to do with unknown ones. It should also say how versions, reserved fields and parameter values behave.

sections.title: Security and Critical Infrastructure
sections.content:
Extensions to critical protocols such as DNS, BGP and HTTP need special care because failures can affect Internet-wide reliability, security or performance. One option is to isolate a new use with a separate port or multicast address, or in a separate process. Extensions should be tested because an implementation may fail to follow the compatibility behavior described in its specification.

An extension's security review should check whether it adds new risks or defeats protections in the base protocol. Adding a handshake to a previously stateless protocol, for example, can create new state for an attacker to exploit. If cryptographic algorithms can be negotiated, designers should avoid allowing negotiation down to an older, less secure algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions to critical protocols can affect many networks, so designers should test them and consider isolating new uses. Security review should check that an extension does not weaken the protections already in place.
